## Source scholarship

Phillips reads the Demodocus song as the ideal aetiology of Greek adultery law: the earliest and fullest narrative display of the legal pattern that the historical poleis institutionalised. On his reading, Hephaestus does not act as a jealous cuckold improvising revenge; he exercises "rights as husband and householder to apprehend and detain Ares" — the self-help seizure of the *moichos* taken in the act, a practice attested across the Greek world and, on the evidence of this very passage, already recognisable by around 700 BCE. The trap, the detention in the bonds, the summoning of witnesses, and the refusal to release until satisfaction: each element corresponds to a step in the legally sanctioned treatment of the adulterer caught *ep' autophōrōi*.

Two philological details carry the argument's precision. First, the hapax μοιχάγρια (Od. 8.332) — formed like ζωάγρια, the price paid for a life spared — names the adulterer's fine: the compensation the captured *moichos* pays for his release. The word exists in Greek exactly once, and it exists as a legal-financial term embedded in this scene; the scene thus contains its own juridical vocabulary. Second, Phillips reads the Poseidon exchange (8.344–58) as formal surety-law (ἐγγύη) in complete procedural sequence: charge stated, penalty demanded, restitution framed against the ἕεδνα (the bride-price Hephaestus paid, 8.318, now the measure of what relation-as-account owes him back), a third party standing surety for payment, and release upon the surety's pledge. Hephaestus's initial refusal — wretched are the pledges of the wretched — and Poseidon's personal guarantee that he will pay if Ares defaults are the recognisable form of the institution, not a courtly ornament.

For the essay this carries two loads, and it is worth stating them exactly. (a) The apparatus's juridical completeness — detection, detention, tribunal of witnesses, fine — is not the essay's projection onto the scene but the scene's own legal anatomy, established by a legal historian on independent grounds (pp. 8–9 of the accessible PDF). (b) The surety exchange is REAL legal form: when the essay argues its trust-closure — the apparatus cannot conclude; only a person standing surety concludes it; Poseidon's ἐγγύη, not the net, releases the bond — that argument rests on an institution Greek law recognises, not on a metaphor. Phillips's wording for all three passages has been verified directly from the accessible PDF; what is missing is not the text but its bibliographic address.

## Essay use

### Source's relevant contribution

Phillips supplies the legal-historical control: the demonstration that Od. 8.266–366 already contains, in its own vocabulary and procedure, the complete juridical apparatus of Greek adultery law — self-help capture, detention, the named fine, and formal surety — so that the essay's "relation-as-account" and "trust-closure" readings stand on attested legal form.

### Licensed essay use

- Establish Hephaestus's trap and detention as the householder's legally recognised self-help against the *moichos* (q001).
- Establish μοιχάγρια (8.332) as the hapax naming the adulterer's fine, on the model of ζωάγρια (q002).
- Establish the Poseidon exchange (8.344–58) as formal ἐγγύη — charge, penalty, restitution against ἕεδνα, surety, release (q003).
- Serve the technology-politics history and the trust thread with the juridical anatomy of the scene.

### Claim boundary

Phillips establishes legal form: the scene's correspondence to Greek adultery and surety law. He makes no claim about technology, surveillance, apparatus in the modern sense, or trust beyond the legal institution. The analogy from ἐγγύη to alignment-era trust displacement — the claim that where the apparatus cannot conclude, a person standing surety concludes it, and what that means now — is the essay's Argued move and may not be attributed to Phillips. Until the venue is resolved, every citation additionally carries the provisional-metadata flag.
